1.pericope_label: Blessed is every one that feareth the Lord: he shall eat the labour of his hands

schools.summary: Augustine turns to a martyr who had none of the domestic blessings named here and argues that he has them perfectly in the Body of the one described, having scorned things present to receive things future.

Calvin calls the psalm an appendage to the one before it, reports how far its maxim stands from common opinion, and makes the second half of the first verse the mark that distinguishes true servants from those who merely boast of fearing God; Gill adds a spiritual sense to the labour of the hands.

Spurgeon finds the two psalms joined by a catch-word, denies outright the opinion that it would be better for a man not to be, and analyses the fear of God into reverence, dread to offend, anxiety to please and entire submission; Henry states the promise of both lives and counts a double blessing in honest work and its undisturbed enjoyment.

Clarke takes the psalm as the second part of the preceding one and supplies a scene in which a visitor pronounces the householder happy, and insists that nobody is exempted from labour but only protected in its fruits.

Ellicott makes the emphasis of the second verse exact and reads the picture of peaceful husbandry as evidence of a settled agricultural people; Keil and Delitzsch argue the pairing of the two psalms from their opening and closing words and compare them to the parables of the treasure and the pearl.

debates: How does this psalm stand to the one before it? Spurgeon finds them joined by a catch-word, since the word rendered happy there is the word rendered blessed here; Keil and Delitzsch turn the same observation into a structural argument, that this psalm follows that one as the second psalm follows the first, one beginning and one ending with the same word, and that the two supplement one another as the parables of the treasure and the pearl do, happiness appearing there as a gift and here as a reward; Calvin calls it an appendage; Clarke makes it the second part of the same poem and supplies a visitor who pronounces the householder happy.

Can the psalm maxim be believed? Calvin says it is so much at variance with the common opinion of men that very few will assent, since the prosperity of the wicked shakes the weak and the adage that it is best not to be born has long been received by almost all; Spurgeon answers that adage directly, denying that this life is a thing upon which rests a curse or that it would be better for the God-fearing man not to be; Augustine argues from a martyr who lacked these blessings and yet has them perfectly in the Body of the one described.
outliers: Calvin instances a temple-robber who, having once had a favourable wind at sea and a prosperous voyage after plundering a shrine, boasted that the gods favour church robbers.

Clarke reconstructs the psalm as a scene, in which the man of many children from the preceding psalm sits at table with his family while a person coming in sees his happy state, speaks of his comforts and predicts every future good.
themes: blessedness promised for this life as well as the next
a maxim contradicted by common opinion
fear of God tested by the keeping of his law
labour required and its fruit secured
a household seen from the doorway

3.pericope_label: Thy wife as a fruitful vine: the children like olive plants, and the blessing out of Zion

schools.summary: Gill takes the vine literally as a tree trained on the sides of a house and reports a Jewish observation about planting it indoors, keeps the closing verbs as promises, and finds the blessing in the word and ordinances of the sanctuary.

Clarke denies that vines were trained on house walls or olives kept in tubs indoors and refers both phrases to the wife and children rather than to the plants, treats the promise as a bargain of a great price for a small consideration, and would render the last clause as a wish; Wesley notes only the number and flourishing of the olive plants.

Ellicott locates the vine in the women quarter of the house and contrasts the good housewife with the idle gossip at her door, requires the optative in the closing verses and holds that the conjunction before the last clause spoils it; Keil and Delitzsch read the closing verbs as imperatives following a promissory future and trace every private blessing to the God who dwells in the holy city.

debates: Is the figure a vine on a wall or a wife in a house? Gill keeps the horticulture and reports a Jewish observation that the vine is the only tree men plant within doors, trained out through a window so that its root is inside and its branches out, whence the modest woman stays within while her children go out; Clarke denies the basis of that, holding that the phrase belongs to the wife and not to the vine, as the table belongs to the children and not to the olive plants, and that vines were not trained on house walls there nor olives kept in tubs indoors; Ellicott places the vine in the inner part of the house and holds the figure no more strained than the table is with olive plants.

How are the closing verses to be construed? Ellicott holds that the optative is plainly required, may the Lord bless thee and mayst thou see, and that the conjunction before the last clause spoils it since the psalm ends in a prayer for peace upon Israel; Clarke agrees for that clause and would render it as a wish; Keil and Delitzsch read imperatives following a promissory future, calling the man to do at once what the promise has made certain; Gill keeps them as promises throughout.
outliers: Gill reports the observation that the vine is the only tree men plant within doors, its root inside the house and its branches trained out through a window, and applies it to the modest wife who remains within while her children go out to work.
Ellicott contrasts the good housewife engaged within at her household duties with the idle gossip who sits at the door of her house on a seat in the high places of the city.
themes: a household described as a garden
a picture drawn before a moral is pointed
blessing traced from the sanctuary to the house
a psalm ending in a prayer for peace
